rows.description: A good friend listens, checks in regularly, offers company and small practical help, and does not lecture or compare pain. They accept that they are not a therapist and nudge toward professional care.
A friend who becomes the only support may feel drained and guilty. Setting kind limits, involving others and looking after own health is necessary to keep helping.
A person supporting someone who says leave me alone feels rejected. Staying gently reachable, sending a low-pressure message and respecting pace, unless there is danger, keeps the door open.

rows.subtype: Adult child seeing a parent low or anxious [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult sees their father withdrawn or mother constantly worried and feels role reversal, fear and guilt. Speaking with love, suggesting a doctor visit and sharing the load with siblings is wiser than silently absorbing it.
graph_context: related mind states: affection, fear, anxiety, guilt

rows.description: An older parent may say I am fine, worry about what people will say or see it as weakness. Framing it as health, involving a trusted family doctor and respecting dignity make acceptance likelier.
graph_context: related mind states: admiration, anxiety, trust

rows.description: A wise family member checks on the parent's sleep, meals and safety, shares tasks and seeks professional help when needed. They protect their own life as well, knowing burnout helps nobody.

A child hears others mock people with mental illness or a classmate with a difference, and learns that struggling is shameful. Adults who speak of feelings and health openly protect the child from hiding pain.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager or family conceals counselling or a diagnosis to avoid log kya kahenge and marriage worries. The secrecy adds loneliness, and choosing trusted people to tell provides relief.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: anxiety, relief, loneliness, trust

rows.description: A peer who hears jokes like I am so OCD or he is mental sees how casual words trivialise real suffering. Gently correcting and speaking respectfully change what people feel safe to say.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A wise adult shares their own experience only when comfortable, treats mental health like physical health and supports others without pity. Each respectful conversation makes it easier for the next person to ask for help.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
